title: Love Righteousness: God Did Not Make Death
sum: The book opens with a call to those who "judge the earth": love righteousness and seek the Lord with a simple heart. God shows himself to those who trust him, and wisdom will not live in a soul that plots evil. Wisdom is a spirit that loves people, but God hears everything, even grumbling and secret slander, because the Spirit of the Lord fills the world.

Then comes the chapter's great claim: "God did not make death" (1:13). He made everything to exist and to be healthy; Hades has no throne on earth; righteousness is immortal. Death is the choice of the ungodly, who call it to them, treat it as a friend and make a pact with it.
readings: Read as wisdom teaching

The chapter reads like Proverbs: a call to rulers, a warning about the tongue, and a contrast between two ways. Its new note is the claim that death is not part of God's design but the result of choosing evil.
Read as an answer to despair
The chapter prepares for the speech of the ungodly in chapter 2. Before they say that death ends all, the book has already said that God made the world for life and that righteousness does not die.

views.C: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Wisdom. The Roman liturgy sings 1:7 in Latin as the entrance chant of Pentecost, reading "the Spirit of the Lord" as the Holy Spirit. Catholic teaching on death as the result of sin draws on Genesis 3 and Romans 5, and readers have long set 1:13 and 2:24 beside them.
views.O: The Orthodox churches count Wisdom among the books of the Old Testament and read it at Vespers. Orthodox writers stress that death is not God's creation but a sickness that entered through sin, which Christ came to destroy; 1:13-14 says this in the book's own words.
views.P: Protestant churches place Wisdom among the Apocrypha, books that may be read but are not used to establish doctrine. Many Protestant readers still value this chapter, since its teaching that God did not make death and that sin brings death agrees with Genesis 3 and Romans 5:12.
views.H: Historical scholars note how Greek the chapter is: the Stoic language of a spirit that "holds all things together" (1:7), Justice as a person (1:8), philanthrōpos (1:6). The author is a Jew writing polished Greek, using the ideas of his culture to defend the faith of Israel.
views.J: Wisdom was not kept in the Jewish Bible, and the rabbis did not preserve it; it survived in the Greek Bible of the church. But its teaching here is Jewish through and through: the God of Israel made the world good, hates death and hears every word, as the Torah and the prophets say (Genesis 1:31; Ezekiel 18:32).

deep.b:
Wisdom says three things in a row: God did not make death (1:13), he made all things to exist and be wholesome (1:14), and the ungodly called death to them (1:16). Then in 2:23-24 it gives the history: God made humans for incorruption, but death entered through the devil's envy, and those on his side experience it.

This is close to Genesis, where death follows disobedience (Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:19), and to Paul: "just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin" (Romans 5:12). The difference is in focus. Paul stresses that death passed to all people. Wisdom stresses that the ungodly choose death by their way of life, while the righteous, even when they die, are "in peace" (3:3). For Wisdom the death that matters is the one the ungodly "experience" (2:24): life cut off from God.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Justice as a quiet answer to the gods
deep.b: This is my own reading, not a scholarly consensus. In 1:8 Wisdom gives Justice (Dikē) a role that Greek readers knew from their poets: the goddess who tracks the guilty. In 1:9 the report goes "to the Lord." The author may be taking a figure from Greek religion and quietly placing it under the one God, as later he will treat the powers of nature as God's servants (5:17-23; 16:24). If so, the opening chapter already shows the book's method: borrow the culture's language, and correct its theology.

echoes: Psalm 2:10; Deuteronomy 6:16; Jeremiah 29:13; Proverbs 8:22-31; Psalm 51:11; Jeremiah 11:20; Revelation 2:23; Jeremiah 23:24; Psalm 139:7; Colossians 1:17; Acts 28:4; Numbers 11:1; 1 Corinthians 10:10; Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:19; Ezekiel 18:32; Romans 5:12; Isaiah 28:15

settings.what: The opening call to the rulers of the earth
settings.by: the book's speaker, who later speaks as the wise king of Israel (7:1-14; 9:7-8), though the book never names him
settings.to: "you who judge the earth": kings and judges of the nations, as in 6:1
settings.when: no occasion is given; it is the start of a teaching addressed to rulers
settings.why: To call the powerful to love righteousness and seek God, and to warn them that God sees all and that the way of evil leads to death. Knowing that the real readers were not kings but Jews in a Greek city changes the reading: it tells a minority under foreign rulers that their faith is the true wisdom of kings.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, under the Ptolemies or early Roman rule (scholars' dates run from about 220 BC to about AD 40). They lived among Greeks, and some of their own people had given up the Law to get ahead.
views: Some read the address as meant also for Gentile rulers and educated Greeks, as an invitation to Israel's God.
Most scholars think the address to kings is a convention, and the book was written to strengthen Jews tempted to give up their faith.

title: The Speech of the Ungodly
sum: The ungodly give their creed. Life is short and ends in nothing; we came to be by accident; the mind is a spark that goes out; no one comes back from Hades; our name will be forgotten. So let us enjoy ourselves: wine, perfume, roses, parties everywhere, because this is all we get.

The speech turns from pleasure to cruelty. Let us crush the poor, the widow and the old; let strength be our law. Then it turns to murder. The righteous man is a nuisance: he accuses us of breaking the Law, calls himself a child of the Lord and boasts that God is his father. Let us torture him and give him a shameful death, and see whether God will rescue him. The author answers: they were blind. They did not know God's mysteries. God made humans for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity, but death came into the world through the devil's envy.
readings: Read as a portrait of unbelief
The speech shows how a life without hope beyond death slides from pleasure into violence. If there is no judgment, the weak have no protector and the righteous are only an annoyance.
Read as prophecy

Christian readers since Augustine have heard in 2:12-20 the passion of Jesus: the claim to be God's son, the mockery, the torture and the shameful death, with the taunt that God should rescue him (Matthew 27:43).
Read as Isaiah retold
Historical scholars see the righteous man as Isaiah's Servant in a new setting: the plot begins with a line from the Greek Isaiah 3:10, and the story of chapters 2-5 follows Isaiah 52:13-53:12.

views.C: Catholic readers have long read 2:12-20 as a prophecy of Christ's passion, as Augustine did. The church accepts that the passage first speaks of the righteous sufferer, and reads it in the light of the cross. 2:23-24 is read with Genesis 3 as teaching that death came through the devil and sin.
views.O: Orthodox writers read the chapter much as the Catholic tradition does: the righteous man foreshadows Christ, and 2:24 names the devil as the source of death. Death, in this reading, is the enemy that Christ destroyed by his own death.
views.P: Protestants do not use Wisdom to establish doctrine, but many see the passage as striking evidence of how Jews before Jesus pictured the righteous sufferer. Some see a providential foreshadowing of the gospel; others caution that Matthew 27:43 draws mainly on Psalm 22.
views.H: Scholars read the ungodly as a type: apostate Jews who have taken up a popular philosophy of pleasure, not one named school. The righteous man is a type of the faithful Jew, built from Isaiah's Servant. 2:24 is among the earliest texts to connect the devil with the death that came in Genesis 3.
views.J: The picture of the scoffers who say life is short and death final has parallels in Jewish wisdom (Ecclesiastes; Psalm 49). The idea of the righteous as God's children and the persecuted faithful as the true Israel belongs to the Judaism of the Maccabean age and after.

deep.b:
The chapter sets two creeds against each other. The ungodly believe: we came by chance, we end in nothing, the soul is a spark, death is sealed (2:1-5). So: enjoy, then oppress, then kill (2:6-20). The author believes: God made the human being for incorruption, as an image of his own eternity, and death entered by the devil's envy (2:23-24). So: the righteous are in God's hand (3:1).

The book's argument is that beliefs about death shape how people treat each other. Paul makes the same point: "If the dead are not raised: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'" (1 Corinthians 15:32). Wisdom lets the reader hear the ungodly's case in their own voice before answering it.

Augustine quotes 2:12-21 and says that in this book "the passion of Christ is most openly prophesied" (City of God 17.20). The likenesses are real: the righteous man claims to know God and to be his child, calls God his father, is tested by insults and torture, and is condemned to a shameful death on the claim that God will rescue him. At the cross the mockers say, "He has put his trust in God, so God should get him free now, if he takes delight in him. After all, he said, 'I am God's Son'" (Matthew 27:43).

Most historical scholars read the passage as a type, not a prediction about one person: "the righteous man" is every faithful Jew persecuted by apostates. Christians can grant this and still read Jesus as the one in whom the type is fulfilled, as they do with Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22. The Plain keeps the passage as Wisdom wrote it.

echoes: Ecclesiastes 2:24; Ecclesiastes 9:7-10; Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32; Exodus 22:22; Isaiah 3:10; Isaiah 52:13; Acts 3:13; Psalm 22:8; Matthew 27:43; Luke 19:44; Genesis 1:26-27; Genesis 3:1-19; Genesis 4:8; Romans 5:12; Revelation 12:9; John 8:44

settings.what: The creed and plot of the ungodly
settings.by: the ungodly, as the author lets them speak
settings.when: in the course of their lives, as they decide how to live and what to do about the righteous man who shames them
settings.why: The author gives them their own voice so readers can see where their beliefs lead: from "death ends all" to pleasure, to cruelty, to murder. Readers tempted to follow such people are shown the end of the road before they take it.

settings.why: To name the error: the ungodly did not know God's hidden plan, that God made humans for incorruption and that death came through the devil, not from God.

title: The Souls of the Righteous Are in God's Hand
sum: The book now opens God's mystery. The souls of the righteous are in God's hand, and no torment touches them. To fools their death looked like a disaster, but they are at peace, and their hope is full of immortality. God tested them like gold in the furnace and accepted them like a whole burnt offering. When their visitation comes they will shine, judge nations and live under the Lord as their king forever.

The ungodly will be punished as their reasoning deserves. Their hope is empty and their families come to nothing. By contrast, the barren woman who is pure and the eunuch who is faithful are blessed: she will have fruit at the visitation of souls, and he will have a share in the Lord's temple better than children. Children of adultery will not last, and a long life brings the unrighteous no honor.
readings: Read as comfort for the bereaved

For those who watched faithful people die young or by violence, the chapter says what death looked like and what it really was: "To foolish eyes they seemed to die" (3:2). This is why the church reads it at funerals.
Read as Jewish hope in Greek words

The chapter speaks of souls and immortality, words of Greek philosophy, but its hope rests on the God of Israel: the souls are in God's hand, not immortal on their own. Whether it also expects the body to rise is debated.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads 3:1-9 in the Mass for the dead. Catholic teaching holds that the soul is created by God and is immortal (Catechism 366), and that the righteous are with God before the resurrection; this chapter is one of the Old Testament texts read in that light. On the soul, see the card below.
views.O: The Orthodox read 3:1-9 at Vespers on the feasts of many saints and martyrs. The righteous dead are alive in God, and the church honors and prays with them. On whether the soul is immortal by nature, see the card below.
views.P: Protestants who do not hold Wisdom as Scripture often still value 3:1-9; the Reformed confession says the souls of the righteous go to God at death, on the basis of other texts. Some Protestants, and the Adventists, hold that the Bible's hope is the resurrection rather than an immortal soul; see the card.
views.H: Scholars see here one of the clearest Jewish statements, before the New Testament, that the righteous dead live with God. They debate how far the author follows Plato's immortal soul and how far he holds to a Jewish hope of judgment and vindication; 3:7-8 has a future, public event.
views.J: The idea that the souls of the righteous are kept by God appears in later Jewish prayer and teaching about the dead, though Wisdom itself was not kept by the rabbis. 3:14 shows a Jewish author taking Isaiah 56 seriously: the faithful eunuch has a place in God's house.

deep.h: Immortal by nature, or by God's gift?
deep.b:
Plato argued, most famously in the Phaedo, that the soul is immortal by its own nature and cannot die. Wisdom uses the word "immortality" (3:4), but it never says the soul is immortal because of what it is. It says the souls of the righteous are "in God's hand" (3:1), that "righteousness is immortal" (1:15), and that God made humans "for incorruption" (2:23): immortality is tied to God and to righteousness, not to the soul alone. In the same book the soul can be "killed" by lies (1:11).

Early Christians argued over the same point. Justin Martyr's teacher, in the Dialogue with Trypho, says the soul is not immortal by nature, since whatever is created could cease to be; it lives "since God wills it to live" (chapters 5-6). Later Christian thought, Catholic and Reformed, has mostly taught that the soul is by nature immortal, while Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses teach that immortality is God's gift to the saved only. The card below sets out the answers.

deep.h: The barren woman and the eunuch
deep.b: The chapter's second half answers a pain the first readers knew. In Israel's old hope, a person lived on through children; to die childless was to be cut off. Isaiah had promised the faithful eunuch "a name that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5) and told the barren one to sing (Isaiah 54:1). Wisdom builds on both: the pure barren woman will have "fruit" at the judgment (3:13), the faithful eunuch "a share in the temple of the Lord" (3:14), and "It is better to have no children and have virtue" (4:1). The Gospels go further still: Jesus speaks of eunuchs "because of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:12).

settings.what: The teaching on the righteous dead and the fate of the ungodly
settings.to: the readers, in reply to the creed of the ungodly in chapter 2
settings.when: after the ungodly have said that death ends all and have killed the righteous man
settings.why: To comfort those who have lost the faithful to early or violent death, and to warn those tempted by the ungodly's way. The suffering of the righteous is a test; their death is peace; their childlessness or early death is no curse. For readers who had seen faithful Jews mocked and wronged, this turned the world's judgment upside down.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, under the Ptolemies or early Roman rule (scholars' dates run from about 220 BC to about AD 40). They lived among Greeks, and some of their own people had given up the Law to get ahead.
views: Some connect the chapter with Jews killed for their faith, as in the Maccabean persecution.
Others think of the everyday pressures of a minority: mockery, lost advantages, early death, childlessness.

traditions.q: "The souls of the righteous are in God's hand" (3:1), and their "hope is full of immortality" (3:4). Is the human soul immortal by its own nature, or does it live on only by God's gift? (Whether the dead are conscious before the resurrection is asked at Revelation 6 and 2 Corinthians 5.)
views: The soul is immortal. The Fifth Lateran Council (session 8, 1513) condemned all who say the intellectual soul is mortal, and taught that it is immortal and belongs to each person. The Catechism teaches that every soul is created directly by God and is immortal: it does not perish when it leaves the body (Catechism 366). Aquinas held the soul incorruptible by nature, though God, who gives all being, could cease to sustain it (Summa Theologiae I, q.75, a.6).

The soul is immortal, but as a gift. John of Damascus calls the soul immortal, yet says it has all its natural qualities "of the grace of the Creator"; of the angels he says they are immortal "not by nature but by grace," because whatever has a beginning would come to its natural end (Exact Exposition 2.3; 2.12).
At death the bodies of men return to dust, but their souls, "which neither die nor sleep", have "an immortal subsistence" and return at once to God (Westminster Confession 32.1).

No soul is immortal by nature. "God, who alone is immortal, will grant eternal life to His redeemed"; until the resurrection, death is "an unconscious state for all people" (Fundamental Beliefs 26). Immortality is conditional, a gift to those saved in Christ.

The soul is the whole living person, not something inside that survives the body, and "the soul can die" (Ezekiel 18:4). Belief in an immortal soul is held to come from Greek philosophy, not the Bible.

title: The Righteous Who Die Young
sum: Childlessness with virtue is better than a large family without it, because virtue is remembered by God and people and wins the crown. The many children of the ungodly are like rootless plants, torn up by the wind, their fruit unripe.

A righteous person who dies young is at rest. True old age is not counted in years: understanding is gray hair, and a spotless life is full age. One man pleased God and was carried off from among sinners (the story of Enoch, unnamed), snatched away so that evil would not corrupt him. People saw it and did not understand that God's grace and care are with his holy ones. The righteous dead will condemn the living ungodly, who will see the wise man's end and not understand. God will laugh at them, cast them down, and their memory will perish. When their sins are counted, their own deeds will accuse them.
readings: Read as consolation
The chapter speaks to grief at an early death: God took the young righteous person away in love, not in anger, and a short life can be complete.
Read as an answer to the old wisdom
Proverbs promised long life to the righteous. Wisdom keeps the hope but moves the reward beyond death, so that an early death is no longer a sign of God's displeasure.

views.C: The Catholic funeral rite reads 4:7-15, often at the funeral of a young person. Catholic readers see in Enoch (4:10) a figure of the righteous taken to God.
views.O: The Orthodox read 4:7-15 at Vespers on the feasts of saints, among them St Nicholas (6 December). The chapter is heard as praise of those whose lives were complete in holiness.
views.P: Protestant readers who do not hold the book as Scripture often still find comfort here; Hebrews 11:5 gives the canonical account of Enoch, who "pleased God" and was carried off.
views.H: Scholars see the chapter as a reply to the older doctrine of reward in this life (Proverbs, Deuteronomy) and a sign of the new hope of life beyond death in the late Second Temple period. The language of the athletic crown (4:2) and of virtue is Greek.
views.J: The early death of the righteous as God's protection appears in Isaiah 57:1-2, and Jewish tradition kept the idea that a righteous person may be taken early for his own good. Rashi says of Enoch that he was righteous but easily swayed, so God "took him away quickly and made him die before his full time" (on Genesis 5:24): the same reading of Enoch as Wisdom 4:10-11. Enoch, taken by God, was a favorite figure of Second Temple Judaism (1 Enoch; Sirach 44:16).

deep.h: Enoch, the model of the young righteous
deep.b: Wisdom never names Enoch, but every phrase points to him. The Greek Genesis says he "pleased God" and that God "moved" him (Genesis 5:24); Wisdom says the man "pleased God" and "was carried off" (4:10). Enoch lived 365 years, a short life beside his fathers' 900 (Genesis 5:23), so he fits the theme: a short life, complete in God's eyes. Wisdom reads his taking as rescue from a wicked world (4:11), which is also how Sirach and Hebrews remember him (Sirach 44:16; Hebrews 11:5). Readers who knew the stories of 1 Enoch would hear more: there Enoch walks with the angels and is shown the judgment of the wicked.

echoes: Proverbs 10:27; Psalm 55:23; Isaiah 57:1-2; Proverbs 16:31; Proverbs 20:29; Genesis 5:21-24; Sirach 44:16; Hebrews 11:5; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Galatians 3:1; Psalm 2:4; Psalm 1:3; Matthew 15:13; 1 Corinthians 9:25; 2 Timothy 4:7-8

settings.what: On the righteous who die young
settings.to: the readers, especially those grieving an early death
settings.why: To answer the fear, built on the older teaching of Proverbs, that an early death means God's displeasure. The righteous young are complete before God and are taken in love.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, under the Ptolemies or early Roman rule (scholars' dates run from about 220 BC to about AD 40). They lived among Greeks, and some of their own people had given up the Law to get ahead.

title: The Judgment Scene and the Divine Warrior
sum: The righteous man stands boldly before those who oppressed him. Seeing him, they are terrified and amazed at his salvation. Groaning, they confess: this is the man we mocked; we thought his life madness and his death a disgrace; how is he counted among the sons of God? We strayed from the way of truth; no light shone for us; our pride and riches have passed like a shadow, like a ship, a bird or an arrow that leaves no trace. We were born and were gone.

The narrator answers: the hope of the ungodly blows away like chaff, but the righteous live forever, and the Lord will crown them and shield them. Then the Lord arms himself for war: zeal as full armor, righteousness as breastplate, judgment as helmet, holiness as shield, anger as sword. Creation fights at his side, with lightning, hail, sea, rivers and a mighty wind, and the thrones of the powerful fall.
readings: Read as the last judgment
The scene is the end of the story begun in chapter 2. The killers see their victim vindicated and confess too late. Christians read it with the scenes of Christ's coming in Matthew 25 and Revelation.
Read as poetry of reversal

The chapter turns everything the ungodly said around: they laughed, now God laughs; they said life leaves no trace, and their own life leaves none; they trusted strength, and the strong are overturned.

views.C: Catholic readers have read the vindicated righteous man as Christ and as the martyrs who share his victory, and 5:15-16 as the crown of the saints. The armor of God in 5:17-20 is read with Ephesians 6.
views.O: The Orthodox read 5:15-6:3 at Vespers on the feasts of saints, among them the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. The crown of 5:16 is the crown of the martyrs and saints.
views.P: Protestant readers know the passage chiefly through Ephesians 6:13-17, where Paul gives believers the armor that Isaiah and Wisdom give to God. Many think Paul knew Wisdom; others think Isaiah 59 is enough to explain his words.
views.H: Scholars see in 5:1-8 the reworking of Isaiah 52:13-53:12: the despised one exalted and his enemies appalled. The divine warrior of 5:17-23 draws on Isaiah 59 and the old war poetry of the Psalms, and prepares for the Exodus chapters, where creation fights for Israel.
views.J: The picture of the persecuted righteous vindicated in a final judgment belongs to the Jewish apocalyptic hope of the time, as in Daniel 12 and 1 Enoch. The Divine Warrior is the God of the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:3).

deep.b: Read together, chapters 2 and 5 tell one story: a righteous man who claims God as his father is mocked, tested and killed; then he stands before his killers, who are stunned and confess that they misjudged him. This is the shape of Isaiah 52:13-53:12, where the Servant is despised and killed and then exalted, while kings fall silent. Wisdom's words come from the Greek Isaiah: the righteous man is a pais (2:13; Isaiah 52:13), the plot begins with Isaiah 3:10, and the onlookers are "astonished" with the verb of Isaiah 52:14 (5:2). So Wisdom is one of the earliest interpreters of Isaiah 53, reading the Servant as the righteous sufferer whom God vindicates. The New Testament reads the same chapter of Jesus (Acts 8:32-35).

Isaiah 59:17 gives the LORD two pieces: righteousness as breastplate and salvation as helmet. Wisdom gives five: zeal as full armor, righteousness as breastplate, judgment as helmet, holiness as shield, anger as sword (5:17-20). Paul gives believers six: truth as belt, righteousness as breastplate, readiness of the good news for the feet, faith as shield, salvation as helmet, the Spirit's word as sword (Ephesians 6:14-17), and calls it all "God's armor" (Ephesians 6:13), using Wisdom's word panoplia. The armor that God wears in Isaiah and Wisdom, Paul puts on the church: the battle is now fought with God's own weapons by his people.

settings.by: the ungodly, after death, at the judgment
settings.when: when they see the righteous man they killed standing vindicated before them
settings.why: Their own confession proves the book's case: the life they chose left no trace, and the man they mocked is among the sons of God. For readers tempted to envy the successful apostates, it shows how that success looks at the end.

settings.what: The righteous crowned and the Lord armed for war
settings.why: To assure the readers that God himself will defend the righteous and overturn the powerful, and so to lead into the warning to kings in chapter 6.
